s01.slug: FRIDAY · 3:40 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE COURTYARD
body: By twenty to four the sun comes in sideways under the olive tree and lays the leaves’ shadows across a blue tarp, and on the tarp, in pieces, is the courtyard sprinkler: a brass head from 1962, three lengths of pipe, a coupling gone green at the threads. Fr. Osei kneels beside it in rubber boots with his sleeves rolled and a pipe wrench in his fist, the wooden rosary swinging off his belt. The sprinkler has been broken as long as Jack has known it, and Osei has never once looked anything but glad to see it.
Jack is here for a hoe. Becca told him to borrow one, and it is not obvious how you ask a priest for a hoe.
“The shed,” Osei says. Becca asked him Wednesday, and told him what for. He points the wrench at the Newman house. “Two nails, beside the Christmas lights. Bring it back. The sprinkler needs it.”
Jack looks at the sprinkler, which has no dirt in it anywhere, and decides it isn’t his department.
In the shed the hoe hangs where he was told, its handle gone silver with age, a strip of masking tape around its neck in Mrs. Fitch’s capitals: NEWMAN · GARDEN · RETURN.

“You know about Isidore?” Osei calls across the courtyard. “He went to Mass every morning and came late to the field, and the other laborers complained to the master, so the master hid in the hedge to catch him.” He sits back on his heels. “And there were angels at the plow. White oxen, the furrows going in straight as a rule, and Isidore on his knees at the end of the row.”

“In 1622,” he goes on, “Gregory the Fifteenth canonized him on the same day as Ignatius, Francis Xavier, Teresa of Ávila and Philip Neri, and the Romans said —” the laugh gets there ahead of him — “the Romans said the Pope had canonized four Spaniards and a saint.” He wipes his eyes on his wrist. “Four Spaniards, and a *saint*. Neri was a Florentine, but Rome had kept him sixty years.”
“So I’m one of the Spaniards.”
“You are the Spaniard who let the angels do his plowing. For a student, I think, a very sound choice.”

body.text: “The board is still set up in my office,” Osei adds, with a nod at his window over the courtyard, “from the night you chose me over the confessional. We will finish the game when the sprinkler is fixed.” He regards the sprinkler.

body: Becca comes out of the Newman house at a quarter to four for a four o’clock, which for Becca is cutting it fine. Something is folded over her forearm with her own straw hat riding on top of it, the hat that lives on the Ranger’s dash. A white lace mantilla hangs over her shoulder, and a little clay water jug swings from one finger.

“Mrs. Fitch let me pick from her basket,” she says, of the mantilla. “She remembers whose it was. She wouldn’t tell me, so it was somebody *interesting*.” She lifts the jug. “Maria de la Cabeza. She was Isidore’s wife. She carried water out to the hired men, and when the Jarama flooded she spread her shawl on it and walked across.” She holds up the mantilla. “I can’t do that part.”
Osei, from the tarp, breaks it to her gently, a doctor with a chart: strictly, Maria was never canonized. Beatified. Rome confirmed her cult in 1697 and left it there.
Becca’s face falls, and for one second the courtyard is a sad place. Then it comes back up. “She’s a saint to *me*.”
Osei laughs from the belly, the wrench across his knees and the rosary rattling on his belt.

The side door of the Newman house bangs and Lena comes out, done with some form for Mrs. Fitch, a Goodwill garment bag zipped to the top over her shoulder. Laney trails her in big sunglasses with a Starbucks iced coffee sweating through its sleeve.
“Lena!” Becca waves the jug. “What are you going as?”
“It’s a *surprise*, Becca. I’ve sworn Laney to silence on her mama’s pageant sash.”
Laney takes the straw out of her mouth. “It’s a *bird*.”
“Laney.”
Lena’s eyes pass over the hoe on Jack’s shoulder and the hat on Becca’s arm, and then the gate clangs behind them.

Becca shakes out what’s on her arm, and it’s a feed sack: heavy cotton, cut and hemmed into a smock with holes for the arms, RATHDRUM FEED & SEED across the back in red gone the color of an old barn, and a length of rope for a belt, run through two brass grommets she set herself.
Jack has been riding under St. Isidore on the Ranger’s sun visor since the night of the football game.
“Well?” Becca holds it up against him by the shoulders to check the length.

response: “I *make* things, Jack.” She turns up the hem to show him the inside seam, folded back on itself and stitched down so not one raw thread shows, because she can’t help it. “Eight kids, one sewing machine. You learn to finish a seam or you wear your brother’s.”

She folds the sack back into its square, sets the hat on top and the stack in his arms, and hangs the jug on his finger for good measure. Behind her Osei is back on his knees on the tarp, humming, threading a washer onto the brass.

choices.text: Put it on over your flannel, right there.
response: He leans the hoe on the olive tree and pulls the sack over his head on the spot, over the flannel, while the Carhartt he came in lies on the bench where he dropped it. The smock comes to his knees. Becca steps in with the rope, cinches it, and ties it off hard, a hay-bale knot with a yank at the end that rocks him on his heels.
Osei glances up from the tarp at the farmer, and past him at the brown canvas on the bench. “Saint Isidore of the Carhartt.”

Becca walks once around him, tugging the shoulders square, then reaches up and sets her straw hat on his head and tips the brim back with a knuckle, to see his face. Then she picks the Carhartt up off the bench, shakes the olive leaves out of it, and hands it to him folded.

choices.text: “Rathdrum Feed & Seed. Finally, a saint with a sponsor.”
response: Becca takes this seriously. “They *are* very generous. Mr. Hollister gives the 4-H every empty sack he has, every spring. We made a *quilt*.”
Osei has to get up off the tarp and sit down on the olive-tree bench with the wrench in his lap until it passes.
Becca folds the sack back into its square with the red letters facing out, so everybody can see who’s paying.

body: “The *staircase*, Delphine.” Theo is bent over his desk on both fists, talking down at his iPhone, which lies on its back on the blotter with a woman in Silver Lake coming out of it at a volume meant for a much larger room. “No. I said *Somerton*. — Lilies up the left rail. Roses down the right. Saints ascend; sinners descend; nobody uses the middle.”
Delphine says something about the fire code.

Room 412 has become a war room. The Ferrante house, three floors of it drawn out on Meridian Pictures letterhead, is taped to the closet door with blue painter’s tape, the staircase circled in red Sharpie so many times the paper has gone soft. By the door sit two cardboard boxes marked HALOS (300) and HORNS (300), and beside them a crate of Venetian masks, white and gold and black, with a Post-it on the slats: FOR THE SHY. Theo’s operation has annexed Jack’s side of the room as far as the crucifix.
“Tell him the cake goes on the *devil’s* side of the table,” Theo says. “He refuses to waste it. Fine. It can work.” Delphine wants to know which side is the devil’s side. Theo closes his eyes.

Laney is cross-legged on the Aerobed under the window in her PI LAM LITTLE shirt with a yellow legal pad on her knee, and when the door opens she flips the pad over against her thigh. Not fast enough. Upside down, in Laney’s round capitals, with a box drawn around it: STAIRCASE · 11:00 · COUPLES.
“The judges,” Laney announces, “will be deducting for not *knocking*.”

body.text: Under Theo’s espresso cup lies a Nepenthe napkin with three couples on it in Theo’s handwriting, the cowboy and the cow crossed out twice, and Jack recognizes his own intelligence work and keeps his mouth shut.

body: “What are you going as?” Jack asks.
“The host,” Theo says, without looking up from Delphine.
“That’s not a costume.”
“It is if you do it correctly.”
“Laney?”
Laney caps her pen. “A lady doesn’t do previews, Jack. Buy a *ticket*.”
Kevin is in the doorway in his navy quarter-zip, holding a flyer by one corner, out from his body, a specimen he’d rather not have touched.

body.title: Student Health, the bulletin board

body: “Health-care workers,” Kevin says. “I am a *future* health-care worker. Every pre-med in Chem 1A is a future health-care worker. We are, I’m told, civilians. Doug is practicing a cough.”

Then he takes in the legal pad against Laney’s thigh, and Laney’s face above it, and Theo’s, bent over the phone, and his smile doesn’t move at all. “Respectfully,” Kevin says, “this is a hostage situation.”
Laney examines the end of her pen. Theo tells Delphine that the roses are to be dethorned, every one, this is not a Passion play.

Then he puts her on hold, mid-word, and turns around for the first time. “Costigan. Tomorrow, four o’clock, the Ferrante house. I have three hundred candles and no one I’d trust with a lighter, and you are the only man I know who can carry a thing without commenting on it.”
“I’m free. I swapped with Hector. He takes Saturday, I work tonight.” Last Saturday, the one he gave up for Big Sur, is still a hole in his month; this one he’s only lending.
“Hector,” Theo says warmly, an old and dear friend of the production, and takes Delphine off hold. “Delphine. I asked for Somerton, and they gave me Del Playa.”
In the doorway Kevin looks at the floor plan with its worn red circle, appears to decide that whatever Somerton is he can live without it, folds the flyer into his pocket, and goes.

The Hobart opens on a rack of coffee cups and lets go a cloud of steam that comes straight up into Jack’s face and fogs the window over the dish station, so that for a few seconds the harbor lights are smears on the glass. Friday is not his night. He took it off Hector, who wanted Saturday, and Friday turns out to be a different restaurant: louder and younger, a booth of girls in cat ears from some pregame demanding fries, two of the harbor guys at the counter already arguing about where they’ll park their trucks tomorrow when the costumes come down the wharf.

Rudy has the transistor on the shelf over the pass, turned low. The World Series is one game apiece — Philadelphia took the opener Wednesday, the Yankees took last night’s three to one — and tomorrow it’s Game 3 in Philadelphia, and tonight, with no game to talk about, a call-in show out of Los Angeles is talking about it anyway. Rudy lays three patties on the flat-top and listens to a man from Encino explain the Yankees’ payroll.
“Bought team,” Rudy says, and flips the patties.

Ray Ochoa is at the counter, and this isn’t his night either: no meatloaf, a windbreaker zipped to the throat, a coffee to go with the lid already on it, a man on his way somewhere who has stopped for one minute to be still.
Gloria comes down the counter with the pot and the pencil through her bun and stops at the end by the dish station, where she can see the room and him. “So. Tomorrow. What are you going as?”
“St. Isidore the Farmer.” Jack sets the rack down on the steel. “A feed sack, a straw hat and a hoe. A girl from Newman sewed it.”
Down the counter, Ray’s head comes up at *farmer*.
Gloria looks Jack over, the steam and the apron and the wet sleeves, and rates him where he stands. “Shoofly,” she says. “Plain, and somebody’s grandmother swears by it.”
“Thanks.”
“What’s the pecan going as?”
“She won’t say.”
Gloria tops off a trucker’s cup on her way past. “Then she’s going as something that’ll ruin you.”

body.text: She comes back with the pot. “You owe Hector a Saturday.” “I’m paying him one.”

body: Ray gets up off the stool with the coffee and turns to face the dish station. “Saint Isidore.” Dry and Westside and tired. “Tomorrow night Marisol PD has every officer it owns on Del Playa and Seacliff, and the county’s lending us deputies. Barricades go up at six-thirty. Four thousand kids, and two hundred of them dressed as Michael Jackson.” He zips the windbreaker to the chin. “Stay off the bluff edges, Saint Isidore. Every Halloween somebody goes off one in Las Olas, and I’m the one who calls the mother.”

choices.text: “The girl I’m seeing is St. Maria. She’ll keep me off the edges.”
response: “Good,” Ray says. “Listen to her.”

Two stools down, Gloria is refilling a sugar dispenser, and the pour stops. “*Seeing*,” she says. She gives Jack one look over the top of the dispenser, screws the cap back on, and that’s all she has to say about it tonight.
Ray leaves a dollar by the register and goes out, and when the door opens the sea lions under the wharf are going at it in the dark like a bar at last call.

choices.text: “Isidore’s a farmer, Sergeant. We don’t do cliffs.”
response: “Farmers fall off everything,” Ray says. “Tractors. Barns. Their own roofs.”
He leaves a dollar on the counter for a coffee that cost a dollar, squares it with one finger, and goes.

Gloria picks up the dollar, writes SHOOFLY on the back of a dead ticket in capitals, and tapes it to the glass of the pie case at the height of Jack’s eyes, where he’ll have to look at it every time he comes out with a rack.
Ray studies him over the coffee lid while the Hobart runs out its cycle and clunks open. Then he nods. “That’s the right answer. You’d be surprised how few people give it.”
He goes out with his coffee into the cold, and the door sighs shut on its closer, and Rudy turns the transistor up a notch so the kitchen can hear the man from Encino lose his argument.

s04.slug: SATURDAY · 1:40 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE LAUNDRY ROOM
body: He hears the upright before he’s off the bottom stair. Somebody in the basement at twenty to two is playing “Just a Closer Walk with Thee,” slow, at the pace of a brass band going to the cemetery, and every time the tune wants the F there’s a soft wooden knock where the note should be, and the tune steps over the hole and goes on.
Jack has three miles of La Flaca in his legs, the Hobart in his hair and a pillowcase of dish-pit clothes over his shoulder.

body.text: He knows whose hands those are.
body.else: Officially, no one in Delgado plays that piano.

body: By the time he comes around the end of the dryers the playing has stopped and the bench is pushed back crooked. Lena is at the laundry room’s ironing board, which has one short leg and rocks at every stroke, with the oatmeal cardigan shoved to her elbows and the iron hissing. On the board is something inside out under a bath towel, for security, and the only part of it out in the air is one sleeve, hanging off the end. Blue. She is ironing the sleeve badly, in short hard strokes, arguing with every wrinkle.
She sees him and whips the towel over the sleeve, and then throws herself across the towel for good measure, the iron held up and away like a torch. “Don’t you *dare* look.”
“I didn’t see anything.”
“You saw a sleeve.”
“I saw blue.”
“Lord have mercy.” She straightens up and pulls the towel square. “It’s a shirtwaist. Nineteen fifty-four. That’s all you get. And if you tell Laney you saw the sleeve, I will know.”
His mother has a picture of Nonna in a shirtwaist, on the porch on Glenwood the summer Eisenhower was president, squinting at whoever held the camera.

They are good at this now. Almost. It has been a week since the porch, and they have a way of doing it: she keeps to her side of the folding table and he keeps to his. He tips the pillowcase into a washer. When he reaches past the can of spray starch for the detergent she pushes the starch across to him by its bottom rim, and her fingers don’t come near his.

body.text: When she leans over the board the tin in her cardigan pocket knocks once against the edge of the table.

body: “It’s Halloween already,” Lena says. “Back home it’s twenty to four and nobody’s gone to bed. Frenchmen Street’s all skeletons. The Marigny. Voodoo Fest has City Park — that’s a mile from our house; you can hear the bass on the porch on Dupre Street if the wind’s right, and Mama shuts the windows and prays the rosary louder.” She runs the iron down a seam and back. “Wes’ll call me from somewhere loud.”

body.text: She sets the iron on its heel. “Daddy asked about you. ‘The one who yells.’” “I yell with respect.” “He knows. That’s why he asked.”

body: She looks at the clock above the door, which says a quarter to two and means a quarter to four, and goes back to the seam.
“We’re doing good,” she says.
“We are.”
And because it’s true, and because tonight she’ll see it anyway, he starts to tell her what he’s going as —

response: She is singing before he gets to the noun. Full voice, Rosary choir, Latin she had before she could spell: “*Salve, Regina, Mater misericordiae* —” He tries again, louder, and she goes louder, the iron raised for emphasis — “*vita, dulcedo, et spes nostra, salve* —” until he quits and leans on the dryer laughing, and she sings on through the valley of tears without mercy. A dryer buzzes right in the middle of *Eia ergo*, and she sings straight through that too.
“I don’t want to know what she picked.” She points the iron at him. “Don’t you *tell* me.”

She gathers the dress up inside the towel, still inside out, posts it into a dry cleaner’s plastic bag without giving him so much as the other cuff, and drapes it over her arm. Passing the upright she plays a bar with her free hand, and the last note is the dead F, and it knocks. “Goodnight, Jack.” She has left the iron on, standing on its heel on the board with its little orange light lit. He pulls the plug out of the wall and stands there with the cord in his hand while the iron ticks, cooling.
He says that instead.

Lena sets the iron on its heel. For a second the only sound is the washer filling. Then she smooths the towel down over the dress, corner to corner, and says it to the shirtwaist: “Then you did it right.” She doesn’t ask what it is.

Passing the upright she plays a bar with her free hand, and the last note is the dead F, and it knocks. “Goodnight, Jack.” She has left the iron on, standing on its heel on the board with its little orange light lit. He pulls the plug out of the wall and stands there with the cord in his hand while the iron ticks, cooling.

choices.text: Say nothing. Take the other end of the ironing board so it stops wobbling.
response: He doesn’t finish it. He comes around the end of the folding table and takes hold of the far end of the ironing board, where the short leg is, and leans his weight on it until it stops rocking.

Lena lets him. She irons the rest of it a hand’s width at a time, folding back the towel only as far as the iron needs and keeping her shoulder to him, and without the wobble the iron goes faster, the steam coming up off the cotton close enough to his hands to feel. She works her way down the whole of it under the towel’s edge, and he holds the board, and the washer fills and churns, and for ten minutes the only talk in the laundry room is the iron hissing when she sets it down. She does the collar last, twice.

She gathers the dress up inside the towel, still inside out, posts it into a dry cleaner’s plastic bag without giving him so much as the other cuff, and drapes it over her arm. Passing the upright she plays a bar with her free hand, and the last note is the dead F, and it knocks. “Goodnight, Jack.” She has left the iron on, standing on its heel on the board with its little orange light lit. He pulls the plug out of the wall and stands there with the cord in his hand while the iron ticks, cooling.

body: Somebody down the hall has propped a door open and put on “Thriller” for the third time since seven, and every time Vincent Price starts laughing a girl in the corridor screams back at him on purpose. In 412 the overhead light is doing its worst. Jack stands in front of Theo’s mirror in a feed sack.

It’s a good feed sack. Becca hemmed it to the knee, and with the rope belt cinched and her straw hat on he looks like a page torn off a seed-company calendar, some month nobody turns to. He reaches back out of habit to put the Kerouac in his pocket, and there isn’t one; St. Isidore had no pockets, so *Big Sur* stays on the desk.

Theo comes out from behind the closet door in a white dinner jacket with the black tie undone on purpose, his hair arranged to suggest he slept on a yacht and didn’t mind. “Jay Gatsby,” he says. “The patron saint of hosts.” He shoots one cuff, then the other. “Also a bootlegger.” He finds Jack in the mirror and approves. “You look wonderful, old sport. You look like a harvest.”

Margot is in the doorway as Joan of Arc: a breastplate of cardboard and silver duct tape over her usual black, a wooden sword through her belt, and her own white-blonde hair, blunt at the jaw, which turns out to have been Joan’s haircut all along. “Burned as a heretic in 1431,” she says, “canonized in 1920. I’m both categories. The Church couldn’t decide either.”

body.text: She says she has come to collect Laney. Then she sits down on the end of Jack’s bed with the sword across her knees, with the look of somebody who knows what’s behind the closet door and has bought a ticket.
body.else: She says she has come to collect Laney, and stays in the doorway with the sword on her shoulder so that it’s clear she isn’t staying.

body: Kevin edges in around her in green scrubs from God knows where, a halo off the top of Theo’s box of three hundred, and a plain white mask, the full-face drugstore kind with nothing painted on it at all. “All Saints,” he says through it. “Every one nobody’s heard of. It’s tomorrow; I’m early.”

Laney has been behind the other closet door for forty minutes, using it as a dressing screen, because Lena locked her out of 217 to change “like it’s the *Manhattan Project*.” The door swings back. Pope Joan: white satin to the floor, three strands of pearls, a cardboard mitre with gold rickrack glued around every edge, and a shepherd’s crook from the Spirit Halloween that moved into the dead Circuit City on Mission. She spreads her arms so the satin hangs. “Margot gave me a footnote, and I made it a *lifestyle*.”
“There was no Pope Joan,” Jack says, from under the hat.
“There were thirteenth-century chroniclers who said there was,” Margot says.
“There were thirteenth-century chroniclers who said a lot of things.”
“I said *legend*, Costigan,” Margot says. “She heard *lifestyle*.”
Laney raps the crook on the linoleum, twice, for order. “Y’all can fight about it at my *coronation*.”

s06.slug: SATURDAY · 8:00 PM · THE FERRANTE HOUSE, DEL PLAYA LANE
body: The Ferrante house is lit like a liner. Floodlights are staked in the bluff-side lawn and every window on three stories is blazing, and up on top the widow’s walk wears an iron rail strung with white bulbs somebody from Silver Lake was paid to string. Somebody’s grandfather built it in 1926 out of white stucco and red tile, and nobody since has been able to heat it.

Inside it smells of lilies and fog-machine glycol. The staircase is the point: one white sweep from the front hall up to a gallery, lilies wired up the left rail and roses down the right, and under it a fog machine breathing a low sweet cloud across the first steps. Theo’s three hundred candles burn in glass jars on every step and every sill; Jack lit them at five with a long-nosed lighter, and has the blister on his thumb to show for it. There’s a girl in black with a clipboard on the landing. There’s a champagne tower under the gallery, five tiers, and a DJ in what used to be the library putting Lady Gaga through the walls. Flanking the door to the rest of the house stand an angel and a devil carved out of ice, each the size of a seventh-grader. The devil is already sweating at the horns. Theo, at the gallery rail in his white jacket, has decided to take this as a review.

At the door two caterers in black hold out two silver bowls, one heaped with glittered halos and one with glittered horns, the plastic-headband kind. On the table behind the bowls is a stack of heavy cream cards, the twins of the one that came under every door in Delgado.

body.title: A card on the table by the door
body.text:
SAINTS & SINNERS
HALO OR HORNS
THE FERRANTE HOUSE · ALL HALLOWS’ EVE

body: On an easel beside the table the planner has propped a sign in white calligraphy, LAST CALL · 1 A.M. · BOTH OF THEM, which has not been explained to anybody.

Becca takes a halo, of course, and settles it on top of the mantilla with the clay jug under her other arm. Kevin already has one. Margot takes the horns. “The 1431 edition.” She looks at the two bowls. “Madonna or whore, sorted at the door, in plastic. Your roommate has reinvented the Church Fathers with an open bar.” Laney takes a halo and sets it on top of the mitre, and then looks at Becca’s, riding on the lace. “Two hats,” she tells Becca sweetly. “We match. I’m the *fun* one.” “You *are*!” Becca says. The caterer with the halos looks at the hoe on Jack’s shoulder, and then at Jack, and holds the bowl a little higher.

response: Becca fits it over the crown of the straw hat for him, her tongue between her teeth, and gets it straight on the second try. Then she steps back to look at the two of them in the black glass of the front window, a farmer and his wife with matching halos, and nods once.
They go on over the hat brim and stick up through the straw. Margot taps one of them with the flat of her sword, approving.
Becca looks at him, and at the horns, and at the feed sack she sewed. “Isidore had a *temper*?”
“He does now.”
He gets the halo over the hat and wedges a horn through the straw on either side of it, and the caterers look at each other.
From the gallery Theo raises his glass to him. “Undecided,” he calls down. “Like my major.”
“Isidore had a hat,” Jack tells the caterer, and touches the brim.
The caterer with the halos looks at him with something close to respect, and lowers the bowl for the next saint in line.

s06a.slug: SATURDAY · 8:01 PM · THE FERRANTE HOUSE, THE FRONT HALL
body: Lena comes in last, alone, at 8:01, out of the dark between the floodlights, and a front hall that has watched a hundred people walk through that door turns around to watch her.

She’s Flannery O’Connor. Black cat-eye glasses that make her eyes enormous. The shirtwaist, which is blue, the blue of the one sleeve in the laundry room, and which fits. The oatmeal cardigan over it, buttoned once at the throat. A stiff little handbag on her wrist, and saddle shoes from the Goodwill half a size too big, which give her walk a careful, churchgoing hitch. Under one arm she has a plush peacock, blue and green, its tail feathers squashed, with a paper tag on a string around its neck that says 57.

body.text: Fifty-seven: the number on the condor’s wing over the Hermitage lot. He turned to show her that bird, and she was already looking.
body.else: It takes Jack a second, and then he has it: the number on the condor’s wing, over the Hermitage lot.

body: At the table she takes a card instead of a headband and drops it in the handbag. Theo leans over the gallery rail. “Miss Broussard. You have to choose.”
“I’m a Southern novelist, Theo. I’m both.”
Then she sees Laney, mitre and crook and pearls. “Pope Joan is a thirteenth-century Dominican with a deadline, cher.”
“She had a *hat*.”

Then she sees Jack. He’s at the foot of the stairs with the hoe, in the feed sack and the straw hat, and Becca is at his elbow in white lace with a clay water jug, and Lena stops in the middle of the front hall with the peacock under her arm.
“Andalusia,” she says.
“That’s in Spain.”
“It’s in Milledgeville, Youngstown.”

And he has it all at once: the peacock letters she read aloud in the van past San Simeon, the farm in Georgia where the birds were. *Whatever she wrote first.* Here he is at the bottom of a staircase in a sack, matching her.
Margot, at his other shoulder in her armor, looks from him to Lena under the horns. “Between the two of you,” she says, “there’s one functioning farm.”

body.text: Theo has come down to the third stair to be a host at Lena. On the way he stops for Becca, takes her free hand and bows over the clay jug. “Miss Lindell. The house is honored.” Laney has drifted up beside him, and she says it low, not quite low enough, with Lena across the hall and out of range: “Farmers have birds.” Theo looks at the peacock. Then he raises both palms and says nothing at all.
body.else: Theo has come down to the third stair to be a host at Lena. On the way he stops for Becca, takes her free hand and bows over the clay jug. “Miss Lindell. The house is honored.” Laney has drifted up beside him and is looking at him. Theo raises both palms.

body: A stranger dressed as Kanye West, shutter shades and all, backs into the middle of the hall with a Canon point-and-shoot and takes their picture, flash and everything. “American *Gothic*! Yo, that’s *sick*.”
Becca blinks off the flash, laughing, and leans in under Jack’s hat brim. “Who’s she?”

choices.text: “Flannery O’Connor. A Catholic writer from Georgia.”
choices.key: Becca asked who Lena was being. You told her: a Catholic writer from Georgia.
response: “Is she a saint?” Becca asks.
Lena, from the middle of the hall, before Jack can answer: “Not yet. She was mean as a snake.”
“Then she’s a *sinner*!” Becca says. “That’s the *theme*!”

choices.key: Becca asked who Lena was being. You said a farmer.
response: Lena doesn’t miss a step. “A *dairy* farmer. Get it right.”
Becca laughs along. If she doesn’t get the joke she isn’t going to ask; she looks glad to be standing where it is.

choices.key: Becca asked who Lena was being. You said her name.
response: It’s just her name. He says it the wrong way for a room with Becca in it.
“I *know* it’s Lena, silly,” Becca says. “Who’s she *being*?”

So Lena tells her, kindly, peafowl and all: Georgia, the farm, a writer on crutches with forty peacocks in the yard who wrote stories about murderers and grandmothers. She tells it to Becca, every word, until the phone rings.

s06b.slug: SATURDAY · 8:04 PM · THE FERRANTE HOUSE, THE STAIRS
body: At 8:04 the LG goes off in the handbag. Lena digs it out from under the card, says, “That’s Wes,” and takes it four steps up the staircase between the lilies with a finger in her other ear and the peacock clamped under her arm. Becca has gone off with Kevin to find out whether the jug will hold actual water. Jack stays at the bottom with one hand on the newel post, on a carved wooden pineapple, with nowhere else he has to be.

“Where *are* you?” Lena says. “Frenchmen? Is that a *tuba*?” She laughs and turns her face into the lilies, away from the DJ. “I’m Flannery O’Connor. … No, *Flannery*. Not a Saintsation, Wesley. The *peacocks*.” And she explains Flannery O’Connor to a boy on Frenchmen Street, Georgia and the farm and the birds and the stories where somebody always gets shot, and she’s funny about it, and she sounds happy. “You’d love it,” she says. “Everybody’s somebody.”

body.text: “Who dat, baby,” she says into the phone, and laughs at whatever comes back.

Jack looks at the roses on the other rail. He thinks, without wanting to, about where a ring spends Halloween: in a drawer somewhere in New Orleans, or riding around Frenchmen Street in a boy’s front pocket, a small hard knot against his leg every time he dances. He gives the thought to the tuba.

body: “I love you too,” Lena says, right on top of him, still laughing. “Go dance.”
She hangs up, her glasses crooked, and comes back down the stairs with the peacock slipping, and drops the phone into the handbag beside the card, and snaps it shut.

s07.slug: SATURDAY · 9:40 PM · THE FERRANTE HOUSE, THE GALLERY
body: By twenty to ten the house is full and the street is coming in the front door in costume, uninvited and unstoppable, and the girl with the clipboard has given up and is dancing. Theo’s people from Los Angeles were due at half past and aren’t here yet. Laney finds Jack on the gallery and takes hold of the feed sack with the hand that isn’t holding the crook. “Roof. *Now*. I’m fixing to bless something.”

Below them the kitchen’s swinging door swings, and in the second it’s open Jack sees Becca and Lena at the caterers’ steel counter, the white mantilla bent toward the cat-eye glasses, their heads together. Then the door swings shut on them.

choices.text: Up to the roof with Laney.

s07a.slug: SATURDAY · 9:50 PM · THE FERRANTE HOUSE, THE WIDOW’S WALK
body: The moon is two nights short of full and high over the water to the southeast, so bright the iron rail throws a shadow on the boards. Up here the wind comes straight in off the water. Down there Del Playa is packed from curb to curb, thousands of people under the streetlights, every one of them somebody else.

Margot is already up, leaning on the rail with her sword. Theo comes up behind them with a bottle of something French by the neck. Laney climbs onto the built-in bench along the street side, gathers her satin, raises the crook over Del Playa Lane, and in a voice that has been trained to reach the back row of a convention center in Arlington, Texas, she says, “*Urbi et orbi*, y’all!”

The street goes up like a stadium. Several hundred people in the road drop to one knee as a joke, a Batman, a bride, and a man in a cardboard box, and Laney gives them the pageant wave, wrist, wrist, elbow, elbow, and they roar.

Two black cars nose through the barricade at the end of the street, where a deputy checks a list against a wristband and waves them on, and they slide up below the house. Theo’s people. Doors open; somebody gets out in a gold dress; somebody else gets out in a cape. Theo looks down at them, and his face goes smooth and pleasant and ten years older, the face Jack saw at his father’s house in Malibu. Laney sees it too. She stops in the middle of a wave with her hand up in the air.
Then a bullhorn goes off below, from a gray car at the curb with a light on its dash: “Your Holiness. Please come down off the roof.”
Laney turns all the way around on the bench. “Is that a *cop* or a *cardinal*?”

body.text: Jack knows the voice from the Anchor counter last night. “That’s Rafi’s dad.”

body: Theo has gone to the far rail. He’s looking past the last houses on Seacliff to the Point, where the old light stands up against the moonlit sea like a dark thumb. Margot goes over and looks where he’s looking.
“Gatsby,” she says. “A man who throws parties for a light across the water.”
“It’s not lit, Margot,” Theo says. “Look.”

choices.text: Help Laney down off the bench.
response: He offers her a hand and she takes both of his shoulders instead and comes down off the bench as if it were a float at the Rose Parade, satin first, and blesses him on the way. “Go in peace, farmer.”
Down on the street the gray car’s bullhorn clicks off. Behind them Theo has already gone down the roof stairs to his guests.
Jack leans over the rail and waves. Down at the curb Ray Ochoa, in a windbreaker, waves back with one finger, tired, and lowers the bullhorn and gets back in the car.
“He *likes* me,” Laney says. Behind them Theo has already gone down the roof stairs to his guests.

choices.text: Go stand at the far rail beside Theo.
response: Margot goes to deal with Laney. Jack goes and stands at the far rail beside Theo, and they stand there, the two of them, with the street roaring behind them and the bottle hanging from Theo’s hand.
After a while Theo says, “Best view in Las Olas. You can see the whole —”
“Ocean.”
“Ocean,” Theo agrees. He hands Jack the bottle, and goes down the roof stairs to greet his guests with the other face back on.

s07b.slug: SATURDAY · 9:50 PM · THE FERRANTE HOUSE, THE KITCHEN
body: The caterers’ kitchen is the only warm room in the Ferrante house: steel counters under fluorescent tubes, eight burners, a radio on top of the refrigerator nobody is listening to, and the devil’s food cake the caterer refused to waste, all of it, cut into squares on four sheet pans on the steel.

body.text: Becca has Lena pinned against the counter, nicely. “Okay. Who is she *really*?”
body.else: Becca has Lena pinned against the counter, nicely. “Okay. Tell me the rest of her.”

body: So Lena tells her. The peacocks, forty of them and then more, and the geese and a pair of swans. The mother who ran the dairy while her daughter wrote in the front room. The crutches. The stories. “Everybody in them is mean,” Lena says, “and God shows up anyway.”
Becca thinks about that, hard. “Does Jack know her? He reads *everybody*.”
“He has her stories,” Lena says. Jack is standing right there, by the swinging door. She straightens the peacock’s tag.

“You’d love ‘Revelation,’” Lena tells Becca, and means it. “There’s a woman with a hog farm, very proud of herself, very proud of her hogs, and she’s sitting in a doctor’s waiting room, and a girl throws a book at her head and tells her the truth about herself.”
Laney comes through the swinging door for ice, crook first, sees the white lace, and stops. “Is that a *tablecloth*?”
“Laney,” Lena says. “Be nice.”
Laney opens her mouth, shuts it, fills a red cup with ice from the caterers’ cooler, and goes back out and up toward the roof with the crook over her shoulder.

At the sink, under the window, Kevin is washing champagne glasses in his mask with his scrub sleeves pushed up. The caterers didn’t ask him to; they keep stepping around him. Through the window over the sink a man’s voice comes in off the street, flattened by a bullhorn, “Your Holiness —” and the rest of it goes under the DJ. Lena glances up at the window, and back at Becca.

choices.text: “She would, Becca. It’s got a hog farm.”
response: Becca has opinions about hogs. She wants the title so she won’t forget it and holds out the back of her hand. Lena takes the ballpoint out of the handbag, holds Becca’s wrist steady against the steel counter, and writes REVELATION across her knuckles in capitals.

choices.text: “Lena reads her better than I do.”
response: “You two and your *books*,” Becca says, and bumps Jack with the jug.
Lena looks at the cake.

choices.text: Go help Kevin with the glasses.
response: Jack takes a caterer’s towel off the oven door and stands beside him at the sink. Kevin washes and Jack dries, glass after glass, a dozen, two dozen, the champagne flutes squeaking in the towel.
Somewhere in the second dozen, through the mask, not looking up from the water, Kevin says, “I’m fine.” Jack hadn’t asked. Kevin hands him the next glass.

s08.slug: SATURDAY · 11:00 PM · THE FERRANTE HOUSE, THE STAIRCASE
body: By eleven the champagne tower is down to its last two tiers, and Jack has had two glasses out of it, which went down like nothing and weren’t. The front hall is packed to the doors.

body.text: He came down from the roof with Laney, who has been talked off the bench and has stationed herself at the gallery rail to bless people coming up the stairs, one at a time, a hand on each head.
body.else: He came out of the kitchen with Becca and Lena into a crowd so thick the three of them get separated in the first ten feet and pushed back together in the next ten. Up on the gallery Laney has got hold of the DJ’s microphone and is telling the house that a policeman has just addressed her, over a bullhorn, as Your Holiness, and that she has decided to take it as an endorsement.

body: The girl with the clipboard has a wireless mic now. She climbs to the landing and announces three categories, to be decided by noise.

Best Sinner goes first and isn’t close. A Sigma Rho senior in an orange jumpsuit, with a placard around his neck that says MADOFF and a briefcase leaking Monopoly money, climbs to the fifth stair with both fists up; the girl reads his name off her card, Brooks Callahan, and the hall roars until the lilies shake. Jack looks at the ice devil instead, the water running off its chin. Brooks works his way up the stairs collecting high fives and stops at the top to flirt with Pope Joan at the gallery rail, and from a few feet down the same rail Theo watches him do it.
Then the girl says, “Best Couple —” and the hall has decided before she gets to the word.
“AMERICAN GOTHIC!”

It means the farmer with the hoe and the woman in the glasses, who are not a couple, who are standing on the second and third stairs because that is where the crowd has pushed them. Lena has the peacock under one arm and in the other hand a flute of Theo’s champagne. Becca is at the bottom of the stairs with her jug, laughing, clapping along with the chant. On the gallery Laney has both hands over her mouth. Theo hasn’t moved at all.

In a gap in the chant Jack hears a small mechanical whir from the landing above him, a clockwork sound. A tall girl with long black hair is up there with a boxy old movie camera, BOLEX in chrome script along its side, and she isn’t filming the staircase. She’s filming him: the straw hat. She winds a little crank on the side and lifts it to her eye again.
From the gallery, Theo, not loud: “Soledad. Don’t.”
She lowers the camera, smiling, and the hall goes on chanting.

choices.key: When the party chanted American Gothic, you stepped down off the stairs.
response: He steps down into the crowd. The hall groans, loud, and keeps right on chanting, at Lena alone on the third stair with her peacock.

She looks out at them for a second. Then she sets her champagne down on the stair, comes down, takes Becca by the hand and Jack by the feed sack, and puts the two of them up where she was, side by side, the hat and the mantilla. She steps down herself and turns to the hall.
“That’s his Maria,” she says. “I’m just a novelist who wandered in.”

choices.text: Reach down for Becca and bring her up yourself.
choices.key: When the party chanted American Gothic, you brought Becca up the stairs yourself. “I’m with Maria.”
response: He reaches down over the newel post and holds out his hand. “She’s Maria,” he says, loud enough for the hall. “I’m with Maria.”
Becca comes up the stairs to him with the jug held out in front of her like a lantern, the mantilla slipping, both of them laughing.
Lena is already stepping down. She sets her champagne on the stair and starts the applause herself, and when Jack finds her face in the crowd she mouths something at him that could be *Good*.

choices.text: Stay where you are, beside Lena.
choices.key: When the party chanted American Gothic, you stayed on the stairs beside Lena until she moved.
response: He doesn’t move. Her sleeve is against the feed sack, blue cotton against feed-sack cotton, and the hall chants it at the two of them, and he stays, and it’s one breath too long and then another.
Lena is the one who moves. She sets her champagne down on the stair, comes down, takes Becca by the hand, brings her up to Jack’s side, and steps down herself to the floor of the hall.
“That’s his Maria,” she says. “I’m just a novelist who wandered in.”

s08b.slug: SATURDAY · 11:15 PM · THE FERRANTE HOUSE, THE STAIRCASE
body: It turns out the hall has never seen a sincere ranch girl in white lace with a water jug before, and it can’t get enough of her. The girl with the mic tries twice to get back to Best Couple and can’t be heard over them, and gives up, and asks for Best Saint instead, and the hall answers her with the name it learned two minutes ago.
“MARIA! MARIA!”

The planner comes up the stairs, a woman in black with a headset, saying “Copy, copy” into it in the voice Jack last heard coming out of Theo’s iPhone about the fire code, and puts a halo spray-painted gold into Becca’s hands. Becca holds it up over her head in both of hers.
“I’ve never won anything that wasn’t a heifer!”
The hall loses its mind. Lena, down on the floor of it, applauds harder than anybody in the house; she has to clamp the peacock under her chin to do it.

body.text: Becca turns on the stair and kisses Jack’s cheek with the gold halo still up in her other hand.
body.else: On her way down Becca hugs Lena, jug and all, and Lena lets her, and hugs her back with the peacock in the way.

body: Best Couple goes, by the hall’s second instinct, to the Joans: Pope Joan and Joan of Arc, side by side at the gallery rail with a crook and a wooden sword. Laney receives it like a coronation, blowing kisses down at the hall with both hands. Margot is appalled. “This is a category error,” she says into the mic the girl holds up to her, and then a laugh gets out of her, a short one, and she shoves it back into her duct-tape gauntlet and glares down at the crowd as if the crowd had done it.
Then Theo raises his glass at the rail beside them, in the white jacket, and the hall, somehow, goes quiet for him.
“Can’t repeat the past?” Theo says. “Tonight, at two o’clock, you can. Once.”

body.text: He tips the glass toward the windows and the dark campus somewhere past them. “And in honor of whoever played the Saints on the Ferrer Tower —” and the DJ drops Louis Armstrong, “When the Saints Go Marching In,” and the hall goes up again.
body.else: He drinks, and the DJ drops Louis Armstrong, “When the Saints Go Marching In,” and the hall goes up again.

body: Lena has her champagne back from the stair. Across the staircase her eyes find Jack’s and hold them for two bars of the trumpet, and then go somewhere else.
Margot’s notebook is somewhere under the armor. She leaves it there.

body.text: Under her breath, to nobody, she says, “One of them was laughing.”

body: Laney comes down off the gallery leading the song with her crook, and half the hall falls in behind her, the Madoff and a lobster and a girl dressed as a traffic cone, and she takes them out the front door into Del Playa Lane at a strut, and the ice devil drips on the tile.

journal.title: Margot Lindqvist
journal.text: Margot Lindqvist. Has a folder on me. Called Lena and me useful idiots for Christian nationalism in front of four hundred people. Made a point about the Euthyphro I still can’t answer. Her mother teaches Classics at Reed. Held a wake for a cigarette on the roof and buried it at sea, for the prose. Had a brother. Her mother was forty-one; the test came back; they’d already picked the name. Anders. March 15, 2000. She’s defended her mother in every room since, and she defended her on the roof. Lena said his name. Doesn’t sleep. My friend. She has a faith column now, in the *Tide*, on a trial basis. If it’s boring they’ll kill it. She told me not to be boring. Came to Big Sur as an observer, for the monks — a functioning patriarchy in its natural habitat. Ran the *Tide*’s Ferrer follow-up from a minivan and wrote nothing down. Sunday at the coffee urn: ‘I’m not writing anything down.’ Halloween: Joan of Arc in duct tape, with her own haircut. Best Couple, with Pope Joan. She called it a category error and laughed anyway.

s09.slug: SATURDAY · 11:40 PM · THE FERRANTE HOUSE, THE FRONT HALL
body: At twenty to twelve Becca finds him at the foot of the staircase with the gold halo in one hand and the mantilla folded over her arm, the jug hooked on one finger. The touch tank is at six; the weekend volunteer still has the swine flu, so Sunday is hers too. Thomas and his neighbors don’t feed themselves.
“Farmer,” she says, about herself, and shrugs, and doesn’t look sorry.

She kisses him goodnight right there at the bottom of the stairs, quick and certain, in front of everybody: the Madoff, the DJ, two caterers, a Pope, and a Georgia novelist sitting on the fourth stair with a stuffed peacock in her lap, who looks at the ice angel. The devil beside it is half gone.

journal.title: Becca Lindell
journal.text: Coeur d’Alene. Seven siblings; wants seven or nine kids, odd numbers, for the tiebreaker. Can butcher a deer — elk too. Has pulled a calf, and it shows. Ran the beach cleanup like a cattle drive and put me on her team. Asked about the scar in the water. Told her mother the cleanup was a date, then asked me if it was. Wrote FRIDAY? on her clipboard, and meant it. Drives her brother Eli’s red Ranger; St. Isidore on the visor. Second date: Friday-night football. Knows downs. Prayed a Glory Be on fourth and one. Learned the First Way on the bleachers and said it back perfectly. Kissed my cheek so there’s no confusion. Third date was mine. I asked. I paid. The elephant seals at Piedras Blancas at sunset, in Kevin’s Odyssey. She knew what every one of them weighed. Nobody’s ever planned a thing for her, she says. She’s been praying for two in the morning. Named a hermit crab Thomas, after the First Way, and asked Fr. Osei whose blessing it was. Works the Marine Lab touch tank Thursday afternoons and Friday at six in the morning — that’s how she signed Thomas out. He’s home; she knows him by the chip in his shell. Mailed Rosie a birthday card with Thomas on it and six true facts on the back, to the address I gave her for her Christmas cards. She does them in October. Has a page on her clipboard for Wes. She’s been praying for him and Lena since September. Her eyes are gray. Brought a survival bag to the library for my midterm, with a clementine for Lena. Prays at two, like always. Took me to *Where the Wild Things Are* at the Rialto; her favorite line is the last one. My mother wrote her a thank-you note. Her list for Halloween says WE SHOULD MATCH!! It’s due Halloween. She says I look at her like homework. She says she’ll wait. Stuck on the touch tank all weekend while we were at Big Sur: the weekend volunteer has the swine flu. Asked me for the monks’ fruitcake for her Grandma Agnes — the only honest fruitcake in America. I handed in my homework six days early. St. Isidore and St. Maria: her first. Early, she said. Nobody’s early but her. Halloween: she sewed my costume out of a Rathdrum Feed & Seed sack. She was St. Maria de la Cabeza in Mrs. Fitch’s lace, with a water jug. Best Saint, by acclamation — a gold halo. Never won anything that wasn’t a heifer. Home at 11:40 for the six o’clock tank; the volunteer still has the flu. ‘Farmer.’

body: She has parked the Ranger out on Ocean Road, past the barricade, nose out under a streetlight, “like a *grown-up*,” by which she means legally. Del Playa’s noise drops behind them until he can only feel it, the bass in the soles of his feet. The moon stands high over the Grove and has whitened the tops of the eucalyptus.

She opens the driver’s door and the dome light comes on, and there on the visor is St. Isidore, a holy card in a plastic sleeve gone pale on the sun side, a man in a brown tunic with a hoe and two angels doing his plowing behind him.
“He’s been on there since August,” Becca says. “I’ve wanted this one all along.”

Jack stands with his hand on the warm roof of the cab while she finds her keys, in the sack she cut and hemmed for him on the Newman machine, with the rope belt through the grommets she set herself, and there isn’t one true thing in him he could say to her out loud.

body.text: She buckles the jug into the passenger seat. “Thomas says hi,” she says. “Thomas doesn’t know it’s Halloween.”
body.else: She buckles the jug into the passenger seat, and the gold halo after it.

body: “Tomorrow, the 9:30? I’ll save you a seat.”
The Ranger’s taillights go off down Ocean Road toward Portolá, and Jack turns around and walks back toward the noise.

s09b.slug: SATURDAY · 11:45 PM · THE FERRANTE HOUSE, THE FRONT STEPS
body: “It’s two blocks to the truck,” she tells him, in case he was going to offer. “I’ve walked cows farther.” She squeezes his hand on the top step, once, hard, a ranch handshake, and goes down into Del Playa.

He watches her from the front steps of the Ferrante house in the feed sack she made him. White lace and a gold halo bob away up the street over a sea of Michael Jacksons, steady, the jug up out of the crush. Once she turns, walking backward, and calls something he can’t hear and then can: “Nine-thirty! I’ll save you a seat!” Then she turns forward again, and the lace gets smaller, and at the corner of Ocean Road he loses her among the costumes and goes on looking at the place anyway.

body.text: He’s halfway back down Del Playa from Ocean Road, threading the crowd with the hoe held upright so it doesn’t take anybody’s eye out, when he sees him.
body.else: He’s still on the front steps, with the hoe across his knees, when he sees him.

body: On the far sidewalk, against the flow, a man in no costume at all is walking a bicycle through the crowd: a stained canvas work jacket, wire glasses, an American Spirit going in the corner of his mouth. Evan Marsh. Jack’s TA. He has stopped dead in the middle of the sidewalk with people breaking around him on both sides, and he’s looking up at the porch of the Ferrante house, where Theo stands under the floodlights in the white dinner jacket, tall and blond and laughing at something one of his LA people has said.
Evan’s face has gone white, the white of the cigarette paper.
“Evan?”
For a second Evan doesn’t hear him. The cigarette has burned down to the filter. Then, without taking his eyes off the porch:

body.text: “Mr. Costigan.”

body: And then: “Who is that?”

response: Evan nods, slowly, still looking at the porch, as though Jack has told him the time and he needs to work out what it means for his train. “Theo,” he says. He drops the cigarette and steps on it.

Evan swings a leg over the bike and pushes off, west, toward Seacliff, through the crowd and the cops and the cups, and is gone into the costumes. Jack looks back up at the porch. Theo has gone inside. Somebody in a gorilla suit hands Jack a beer he didn’t ask for, and the bass finds him again, and the party takes him back.
Evan doesn’t smile. “Right,” he says. He drops the cigarette and steps on it, looking at the porch the whole time.

Evan looks at him then, for the first time. “No reason,” he says.

s11.slug: SUNDAY · 12:35 AM · THE FERRANTE HOUSE, THE WIDOW’S WALK
body: The moon has come west since ten. It hangs over the channel now, lopsided by a sliver, so bright that the white bulbs somebody from Silver Lake strung along the iron rail have nothing left to do, and every roof on Del Playa looks wet. Jack comes up the last flight for air, the steep one, servants’ stairs, and the cold off the water gets in under the feed sack at once.

Margot is coming down as he comes up, the wooden sword under one arm and her horns in her hand. She stops a step above him, so that for the length of the sentence she has the height. “Your host left his own party at twelve-thirty,” she says. “Out the back gate. Toward Seacliff.”

body.text: “And Kevin hasn’t taken that mask off since Delgado.”

body: She goes on down past him in a creak of cardboard and duct tape, toward the noise.

Lena is up here alone. She’s on the iron bench at the east rail, the street side, with the peacock beside her and the O’Connor handbag on her knee and Flannery’s glasses pushed up into her hair, and she’s holding a flute of Theo’s champagne out over Del Playa at arm’s length, as if it might go off. It’s the flute she’s been carrying since nine. It’s still full to the same line.
“Laney blessed the DJ,” she says, without turning around. “And the ice devil, for all the good it did him. And a boy from Hillel who said it couldn’t hurt.”

Jack sits down on the other end of the bench, with the peacock’s tail in the way. Below them four thousand people are doing whatever they want in the road. He takes the Reds and the Bic out of the band of Becca’s straw hat, where they have ridden all night, and shakes one out.

body.text: Lena’s eyes go to the cigarette, and then down to the handbag on her knee, where the tin is.
body.else: Lena’s eyes go to the cigarette.

choices.key: On the widow’s walk Lena asked if this was the occasion. Reliquary No. 7.

journal.title: The Reliquary
journal.text: An Altoids tin from a pea-soup restaurant in Buellton. RELIQUARY on the lid. No. 1: the Lighthouse. No. 2: Malibu, before breakfast. No. 3: the harbor — she smoked half of it first. No. 4: a clove, on the Delgado roof, at a wake. By dispensation. Do not ask. No. 5: the Ferrer Tower, in the bells. No. 6: Lucia, a motel porch, under the stars — on the back of the receipt. No. 7: Del Playa, on the widow’s walk, on the back of a HALO OR HORNS card. All Hallows — the occasion.

“Is this the occasion?” Lena says.

She sets the flute down on the bench, leans past the peacock, and takes it out of his mouth, and puts it out on the iron rail, turning it against the paint until it’s dead. body: They go down the back stairs at five to one with the peacock and the hoe. From the turn of the stairs Jack can see across into the front hall: Laney three steps up the grand staircase above Brooks Callahan, blessing his orange jumpsuit whether he wants it or not, and Kevin by the front door in his white mask with his arms folded, counting heads. At the bottom two caterers in black are smoking by the bins. One of them, the halo caterer, raises his cigarette to the hoe. No one stops them. They go out by the side gate into Del Playa.

Las Olas has turned out for Halloween like a town at the end of a war. The road is full from the bluff-side houses to the ones across it, thousands: Michael Jacksons by the hundred, single gloves and fedoras and red jackets with too many zippers, because *This Is It* opened Wednesday and he has been dead four months; Balloon Boys in tinfoil saucers; a Kanye interrupting a Taylor every twenty feet, the same joke in a hundred mouths; a knot of Snuggies chanting something from inside their sleeves; a man dressed, with real commitment, as the swine flu. Marisol PD walks the middle of the road in reflective vests. There are red cups in the gutters and on the porch rails and stacked into pyramids on the roofs, and on one roof somebody’s sound system is playing the Yeah Yeah Yeahs loud enough to shake the gutters, Karen O ordering the street to dance, and the street doing it.
Through it, west, on the bluff side, go a farmer and a Georgia novelist.

It’s Lena who starts it. She brings Flannery’s glasses down out of her hair and settles them on her nose, tucks the peacock under her arm like a pocketbook, and from the neck up she is somebody else. “Mr. Isidore,” she says, in a Georgia that keeps sliding back toward the Mississippi when she isn’t watching it, “I don’t believe we’ve been introduced.”
Jack’s Spanish farmer comes out by way of Youngstown, a peasant from outside Madrid who learned his English on the line at Lordstown. “Miss O’Connor. What brings you to California?”
“I came to see if what they say about it is true, Mr. Isidore.” She looks down her nose at four thousand people in costume. “There are no *peacocks*.”
“There’s a man dressed as the swine flu.”
“I saw him. I’d like to put him in a story.” They pass it. “And then gore him with a bull.”
“Lovingly.”
“It’s the only way I know how.” Half a block on, eyes front: “Is that a hoe you’re carrying, Mr. Isidore, or are you just —”
“It’s a hoe, Miss O’Connor.”
“I was afraid of that.”

“Back home in Madrid,” says Mr. Isidore, “the angels do the plowing. Union angels. Local Eleven-Twelve. An hour for lunch, nothing after four, and if the master so much as looks at them they file a grievance with God.”
“And does God settle?”
“Every time, Miss O’Connor. Who’s He gonna get instead? Methodists?”
A girl in angel wings is being sick, very neatly, into a hydrangea. Miss O’Connor steps around her without comment, her shoulders shaking. Mr. Isidore lifts his hat.
“Do you have a beau, Miss O’Connor?”
“I have a correspondent,” she says. “He calls at eight-oh-four.” She doesn’t miss a step. “Do you have a wife, Mr. Isidore?”
“I have a Maria. She crosses rivers.”

body.text: They walk on like that, Lena along the fences and Jack out by the curb, the sidewalk left to whoever wants it, and the costumes do the talking.

body: The crowd makes it an hour’s walk to the end of the street. At the cliff end, where the houses run out of party, one porch is dark. Hale is sitting out on it in a canvas chair with a glass, a deaf old greyhound asleep across the doormat like a draft stopper, watching Las Olas go past in costume. He has heard the last half block from his porch. “Mr. Isidore,” he says. “Miss O’Connor. A Spanish farmer and a Georgia Catholic: the Counter-Reformation and the Confederacy, out for a walk.”
“She’d have eaten you for breakfast, Professor,” Lena says.
“I’d have been honored.”

body: Past Hale’s, the road ends at a guardrail and the top of the wooden stairs that switchback down to Shipwreck Cove, still wearing last year’s dead Christmas lights. Somebody has a fire going on the sand below. Lena sits on the top step to shake a pebble out of a saddle shoe that’s a half size too big, and Jack pulls the RAZR out from under the rope belt for the time.
It says 1:59. He watches it. Lena, seeing him watch it, digs the LG out of the handbag and watches hers.
The minute turns, and the RAZR says 1:00. A second later, in her hand, so does the LG.
“We get it again,” Lena says, in her own voice.
“The whole thing?”
“The whole thing, Youngstown.”
She puts the shoe back on and stands, and the Georgia comes back into her mouth, and she waits to see what Mr. Isidore will do with it.

s13.slug: SUNDAY · 1:05 AM (AGAIN) · SEACLIFF ROAD, THE LAST HOUSE
body: The LG goes off in the handbag at five past one, the second five past one, as they come around onto Seacliff. Lena fishes it out. “It’s Kevin,” she says, and answers it walking. “Kevin. — Say it again, I can’t hear you. — She *what*?”
She stops on the curb.
“When? — Twenty-five minutes ago? Which one-forty?” She listens. “With who? … What wall.” A longer listen, her finger in her other ear. “Okay. Okay. Go. Call me.”

She takes the phone down and tells him fast, in order: Laney left the party with three Pi Lam pledges at one-forty — “the first one-forty” — and a sophomore dressed as a nun told Kevin they were walking the wall. *It’s tradition.* Laney’s BlackBerry goes straight to voicemail. Kevin’s going to check Lupe’s.
Then she puts the phone against her mouth and holds it there.
Jack has heard about that wall. Pledges used to walk it, on the outside.

They run west. Down the middle of Seacliff, past the surf rentals with boards racked on the porches and the party thinning to porch lights and stragglers. Ten steps in Lena kicks off the Goodwill saddle shoes, scoops them up without stopping, and runs barefoot on the asphalt with the shoes in one hand and the peacock clamped under the other arm. Jack runs with the hoe, because he has forgotten he’s holding it.

The Lighthouse is the last house. It has a smaller party of its own going on the back porch, orange lights and somebody’s iPod, and nobody on the porch looks up as the two of them go down the side yard to the chain-link fence and the gap where the post rotted, and the path beyond it, pale as chalk.
At the gap Lena stops, a step short of it, with her shoes in one hand and the bird under her arm, and her free hand goes up to the chain at the collar of the shirtwaist.
“Go,” she says. “Please, Jack. I’ll keep calling her. *Go*.”
“I’m not asking,” he says.
“I know.”
She stands at the gap in the moonlight with her shoes in her hand, and he goes.

The path runs out along the top of the bluff through ice plant that squeaks under his shoes, and the sea is loud below the edge of it, working at the reef in the dark. The moon is bright enough that his shadow goes out ahead of him on the dirt, a man in a hat with a hoe, and gets to every bend first. Behind him the Lighthouse porch thins to one song and then to nothing. Up here there’s the wind, and the ice plant, and somewhere below on the rocks a sea lion complaining about all of it.
“Laney!” The wind takes it off toward the hills. He tries again. “*Laney!*” Only the water answers.

The old light comes up out of the headland, a squat white tower with its lamp room boarded over, smaller than it looks from Del Playa, with a padlock on its iron door gone orange from the salt. There’s a county sign on a post, and he can read it without a light: POINT MARISOL LIGHT, 1890. DECOMMISSIONED 1967.
Past it the land runs out at a low stone wall, fieldstone, knee-high on his side. On the other side there is no other side.

body.text: At the wall stands a white wooden cross with a name burned into the crossbar. NORA. He knows the name from a brass plate at St. Brendan’s and from Priya, and he knows where he is.
body.else: At the wall stands a white wooden cross with a name burned into the crossbar. NORA.

body: At its foot is a bunch of something that was flowers two weeks ago, brown now, tied with kitchen string.

body.text: The last edge he stood at was a rail at Bixby, with her beside him.

body: No Laney. No pledges.
Theo.

He’s at the wall in the white dinner jacket, the only white thing on the headland besides the cross and the light, both hands flat on the stones, leaning out over them to look down at the water. There’s a bottle on the ground by his foot, a Krug, mostly gone. The wind has his hair every which way and he hasn’t done anything about it, and that, more than the bottle, is what Jack can’t stand to look at.
“Theo.”
He doesn’t turn around.
“Don’t. Okay? Just — not there.”
The wind comes up over the edge and flattens the ice plant and lets it go. Below the wall, a long way down, the reef goes white, and black, and white again, slower than seems right.

Jack stops on the path. His friend is drunk at the top of a seventy-foot drop in the middle of the night, leaning out, and Jack’s body has it before his head does, in the backs of the knees and in the hands. The hoe gets heavy in his hand. Jack has stood at edges himself, and sat on a few, for the hell of it. He has never had to stand behind somebody else at one. It’s a different thing, and his knees knew it before he did.

journal.title: The Point
journal.text: A cliff, according to Priya. Nobody goes there after dark. Her rule, not the school’s. Now I know whose rule it is. Went up on Halloween, the second one o’clock, looking for Laney. The old light, dark since 1967. A low stone wall, knee-high on my side and nothing on the other. A white cross: NORA. Somebody’s flowers, two weeks dead, on kitchen string.

response: He stays where he is, ten feet back from the stones, and talks. “Laney’s missing. She went off with some pledges. Somebody said the wall.”
Theo’s hands stay where they are. “She’ll be at Lupe’s,” he says. “She always ends up at Lupe’s.”
It takes a long time. Jack keeps talking, about Kevin and the phone and Lena at the fence and three pledges in wimples and anything else he can think of, and doesn’t take a step.
“You’re babbling, Costigan.”
“Yeah.”
“Keep going.”
He does, and in the end Theo comes away from the wall on his own: one hand, then the other. He straightens. He picks up the bottle and looks at it, and puts it down again.

response: He goes and stands beside him on the land side and puts a hand on the stones. They’re cold, and gritty with salt, and on the other side they go straight down into nothing he wants to look at.
“I said not there,” Theo says, without looking at him.
Jack stays.
Theo looks at him then, at Jack’s hand on the wall, and straightens up off the stones, and steps back from them, one step and another. “Come away from there, Costigan.” And Jack does.

response: He sits up on the wall. He’s sat on worse with less reason. The stones are cold through the sack and there’s nothing at his back but air and the noise of the water, and he says, “Theo, come on —”

Theo has him by the feed sack before he finishes, both fists in the cloth at his chest and a heave that starts somewhere down in his legs, and Jack comes off the wall on the land side and they go down together in the ice plant, hard, the hat gone, the hoe somewhere, Theo on top of him.

Theo doesn’t let go. His hands are shaking in the sack, both of them, and they keep shaking, and he keeps hold. The ice plant is wet under Jack’s back. He can feel Theo’s knuckles against his breastbone through the cotton, going and going.
After a long time Theo says, “Don’t do that.” Then nothing; the sea, and his hands.

response: He sits down in the dirt at the foot of the wall with his back to the stones and his face to the land. The hoe goes across his knees. From down here there’s the old light, and the path back, and the orange glow of Las Olas over the bluff, and nothing of the sea but its noise.
He waits.
After a while Theo takes his hands off the wall. He slides down it beside Jack, back to the stones, knees up, and sets the bottle in the dirt by their feet, and they both look at the lighthouse.
“Laney?” Theo says at last.
“Missing.”
“Lupe’s.”

body: They go down the path together, Theo in front, saying nothing. He wipes his palms on the white jacket as he walks and leaves two gray prints on it. Del Playa comes back to them a piece at a time on the way down: the bass first, then a siren somewhere inland, then somebody on the Lighthouse porch singing along to Journey, badly, with feeling. At the gap in the Lighthouse fence, before the streetlight on Seacliff can find them, Theo stops.
“Tell them I was looking for Laney,” he says.

journal.title: Theo Vance
journal.text: Roommate. Drives his grandfather’s car like a getaway. His father calls him Teddy and stays six minutes. Heard my brother’s voice and didn’t ask. Loves *Point Break* with no irony at all. Poppy texts him at midnight. The Big Sur Expedition, on his father’s letterhead. Called the Anchor and got my Saturday covered before I could say I work Saturdays. Bought six used copies of Kerouac off the cart at Driftwood. Halloween: threw the party of the year as Gatsby. Left it at twelve-thirty by the back gate. Found him at the wall at the Point at one in the morning, the second one. He said not there.

s15.slug: SUNDAY · 1:35 AM (AGAIN) · SEACLIFF ROAD, UNDER THE STREETLIGHT
body: Lena is under the one streetlight in front of the Lighthouse with the LG and the saddle shoes in one hand and the peacock under the other arm. She doesn’t come to meet him. She stays under the light and makes him come to her, and before he reaches the curb she has told him that she called Laney eleven times and Kevin twice, as a charge against Las Olas generally.
“She’s eating a *burrito*, Jack.”

“I stood at that fence and called her eleven times and said every prayer I know, and the Memorare twice, and she was in line at Lupe’s with a dead phone, ordering *guacamole*.” She presses the heel of the hand with the phone in it against her eyes, shoes and all, for a second. “Lord. I’m going to hug her, and then I’m going to kill her.”
She looks him over from the hat to the shoes as if she’s counting him. Her ear is red from the phone. The hand with the shoes in it is shaking.
Then she looks past him, up the path, into the dark where it goes. “Was anybody up there?”

s15a.slug: SUNDAY · 1:38 AM (AGAIN) · SEACLIFF ROAD, WALKING EAST
body: They start east toward Lupe’s down the middle of Seacliff, where the party has thinned to stragglers and red cups. Lena walks the yellow line. There’s grit on her ankles from the road, and she doesn’t seem to feel it.

Jack still has the wall in his knees, and in his hands; he’s carrying the hoe in both of them, as if it might get away. He says it walking. “Maybe that’s what it takes, for some people. Somebody standing at an edge. Then they wake up.” And because she’s dressed as the woman who said it best: “Your girl would back me. Violence is strangely capable of returning her characters to reality. Her words, more or less.”
Lena rounds on him under the next streetlight, Flannery’s glasses flashing.
“I came as her,” she says. “I never said she was right.”

She takes it apart walking backward in front of him. O’Connor said it herself, in *Mystery and Manners*: *to the hard of hearing you shout, and for the almost-blind you draw large and startling figures.* “That’s a novelist with a megaphone, Jack. That’s how you get the attention of people who won’t listen to a book. It isn’t how God works. She was shouting at *us*. God doesn’t have to.”

“Grace doesn’t tear nature down to build on it, Jack. It perfects it. Thomas, first question of the *Summa*: *gratia non tollit naturam, sed perficit.* You don’t have to blow the house up to move in. He has a key.”

choices.text: “He shouted at Augustine. Augustine’s word, not mine.”
response: He has the Pine-Coffin nearly by heart. “*You called me; you cried aloud to me; you broke my barrier of deafness.* Book Ten. He shouted.”
“He shouted,” Lena says. “He didn’t *shoot*. And Monica was on her knees for him for seventeen years before he heard a thing. That isn’t a gunshot, Jack. That’s a *mother*.”

choices.text: “You came dressed as a woman who bought birds to annoy her mother. Don’t tell me about gentle.”
response: She laughs, in the middle of Seacliff Road, and has to stop walking backward to do it.
“She bought them because she *loved* them, Costigan. The mother was a side benefit.” The point is his; she waves it off with the shoes.
She stops walking backward. Three steps go by before she uses it.
“Don’t be nice to me,” she says. “I’m *winning*.”

choices.text: “You won’t even walk up a path.”
response: It’s true, and it wins the point. She opens her mouth, and closes it.
She stops walking backward. She steps off the yellow line to the far side of the road and walks on over there. “Mr. Costigan,” she says.

s15b.slug: SUNDAY · 1:45 AM (AGAIN) · SEACLIFF ROAD, WALKING EAST
body: They pass the Alpha Tau house, where a boy in a toga is asleep on the lawn with his laurel wreath down over one eye and two friends are drawing on him with a Sharpie, slowly, tongues out. Lena steps over a Solo cup without looking at it. She gets to the Misfit before he can.

In Georgia, quoting: “*‘She would of been a good woman,’ The Misfit said, ‘if it had been somebody there to shoot her every minute of her life.’*” Then, as Lena: “That’s the *Misfit*, Jack. A man with a gun says it. You want your theology from the man with the gun?”
“My grandmother didn’t need four days of water to be good. She was good.”

“And don’t tell me it took the storm to make her, because I knew her before. She was good on a Tuesday. She was good in the checkout line at Schwegmann’s. Nobody had to hold a gun on her. If grace only comes like that, Jack, then it skipped her, and I won’t have it. I won’t have a God who couldn’t find my grandmother till the water came up.”

choices.text: “The Misfit’s wrong about everything but that.”
response: “*The kingdom of heaven suffereth violence*,” Jack says, “*and the violent bear it away.* Matthew eleven, the Douay. She named a book after it. She meant it.”
“She meant it about *fiction*,” Lena says, and walks faster.

Lena walks half a block on it. Then: “She made the roux dark, and she never said a mean word about anybody, and she died in the dark anyway. And I’m not calling that grace.” Her bare feet on the road. “I’m not.”

choices.text: “Maybe the flood wasn’t the grace. Maybe the boat was.”
response: Lena goes quiet.
“…Maybe,” she says.

response.text: He wishes he hadn’t said *boat*. There’s a knocking under a roofline on Pauger Street in his head, the one a boy in a flatboat couldn’t reach, and he keeps it.

response: “Yes,” Lena says. “It was.”
She crosses back over the yellow line to his side of the road, and walks there.

body: Seacliff Road goes on east under its streetlights, a pool of orange and then dark and then the next, and they walk through them, in and out. In the dark stretches he can hear her bare feet on the asphalt and the peacock’s plastic eyes ticking against the clasp of the handbag. In the light he can see her face, and she’s still arguing; she walks a little ahead, as if the rest of it is somewhere up the road and she means to get there first. Two blocks short of Lupe’s he says it.

body.text: “Have you ever been up there?” he asks. “To the wall?”
body.else: “You’ve never stood up there,” he says. “You don’t know what it looks like from the wall.”

body: “No,” Lena says. “I never have.” Her fingers are on the medal at the collar of the shirtwaist.

“A week ago at the monks. Bartimaeus. The crowd telling the blind man to hush, and Jesus stops the road. He *asked* him, Jack. *What do you want me to do for you?* He knew. Anybody could see what the man wanted. He asked anyway.” She has the peacock by the neck now. “If God has to push me off a cliff to save me, I don’t want it that way. I want to be *asked*.”

response: He knows one way it comes, and keeps it behind his teeth.
“Then He’s rude,” Lena says, “and I’ll tell Him so to His face.”

This far east the street is empty. A block back somebody’s porch speakers are playing something slow, a girl and a boy taking turns on it, and nobody on the porch is listening. There’s Lupe’s generator, and the sea under the bluff, and the minute.
Then she takes off Flannery’s glasses and holds them folded in her hand.

Jack wants her. It isn’t complicated and it isn’t new. It’s Lena, barefoot on Seacliff Road at a minute to two, with the grit of the road on her ankles and her shoes in her hand and nothing on her face but her face: the marks the glasses left on either side of her nose, a fleck of somebody’s glitter at her temple, her mouth a little open from the last block. journal.title: Duels with Lena
journal.text: Two–one after Labor Day; she paid her Sunday. Three–one after moral luck: mine; she said I argued it like it was mine. Now four–one. Friendship: mine, arguing both sides. She said she’d never forgive me. Wednesday she said she forgives me. I’d rather she hadn’t. Unofficial, the laundry room, midnight on her feast, no referee — the Little Way: Thérèse, on points. Unofficial, the Brick, four in the morning, no referee — on the heart: nobody won. Official, Hale’s seminar, the day after the Anglicans — on leaving: mine. Five–one. Hale says I argued for leaving like a man who’s never been allowed to. Unofficial, Seacliff Road, Halloween, the hour that happened twice, no referee — on grace: hers, by forfeit. I said the thing about the path. At a minute to two I took it back.
